§9.1.5 Is This Even a Table

📄 Page rule — applied from the page alone

tables-is-this-even-a-table · tables detection boundaries

✅ Normative

A region MUST be rendered as a table when, and only when, its rows and columns encode a relation — when the position of a value in the grid is what gives the value its meaning. A region that encodes no relation MUST NOT be rendered as a table.

This is the first decision about a region, and every other table rule depends on it. A single page often shows the whole spectrum at once: real grids, gridded legends, ungridded label: value spec stacks, address blocks, and two-column prose that looks like a grid but is not.

Same page, three regions:

┌─────────────┬───────────────┐      Motor: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← ungridded spec
│ (1) Premium │ Base rate …   │      Speed: 3-speed              stack: table? text?
│ (2) Losses  │ Incurred …    │
└─────────────┴───────────────┘      Acme Corp
  ↑ gridded legend: table?           123 Main St    ← address block: never a table

The test

The question is: would this be a <table> in well-written HTML, or a <div> positioned with CSS?

A border alone does not make a region a table, and alignment alone is not always enough either. The relation decides.

Strong evidence it is a table Strong evidence it is not
explicit row and column headers running prose, however neatly it is set in columns
repeated records under a shared schema address blocks
a printed grid, or consistent column tracks running down the block text sitting beside a logo
a legend printed as label/definition records inside a grid decorative alignment with no record schema behind it

❌ Counter-sample — 4x

The page starts straight into data rows with no header row. Column meaning has to be inferred from the values, which is the edge of the relation test: repeated records under one schema still make it a table, and the output MUST NOT invent the missing header row.

Legends and static key-value references are tables

The "Column | Description" box under a rate grid, explaining what (1)–(11) mean, MUST be rendered as a table.

| Column | Description     |
| (1)    | Earned premium  |
| (2)    | Incurred claims |

It looks decorative, but it maps one thing to another, and a mapping is a relation. Omitting it drops real content off the page.

Prose and address blocks are never tables

Two-column running prose only looks like a grid — its columns carry no meaning, they are a typesetting choice. The same holds for an address block, or a caption stacked beside an image. These MUST NOT be rendered as tables.

❌ Counter-sample — 10k

A 10-K cover: Yes ✓ No check-mark lines and an address block, both column-shaped, neither tabular. The genuine table is the small Title of each class / Trading Symbols / Exchange grid.

Label / value blocks without a grid

Two columns of labels and values with no ruled grid are a table or key-value content depending on the data, not the layout. The same two whitespace tracks can hold either.

The rows are… Rendering Examples
Records of one kind — every label is paired with the same kind of value (an amount per component, a factor per year) a table, even with no header row and no ruled grid a Working Capital panel (see Borderless Whitespace Tables§9.1.1); the Trend Factors block of wwa below
Different kinds of fact — each label names its own field (a filing number, a state, a date) key-value content — see Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 filing metadata, a spec sheet, a biography's Name: / Affiliation: lines
Headline figures — labelled KPIs set as tiles or a highlight panel stat tiles — see Stat Tiles§5.11 Out-of-home +26.5%

A bold label with its value flowing after it — blower spec sheets and similar — is the second kind.

**Motor**: 1/2 HP, 115V      ← no ruled grid, value flows after the label
**Airflow**: 1,200 CFM

A stack whose labels name different kinds of fact MUST NOT be rendered as a table unless a ruled grid is printed around it; it is key-value content, and every line of it MUST still appear in the output. A stack whose rows are records of one kind MUST be rendered as a table.

Form intertwined with a grid

Rate-filing pages that are half form, half table.

Insurer: [blank]   NAIC #: [blank]     ← form fields…
| Year | Rate change |
| 2024 | +4.2%       |               ← …and a genuine grid, same page

The ruled grid region MUST be rendered as a table and the form fields as key-value content, so that nothing printed is lost. The table MUST NOT be stretched to swallow the form fields, and the grid MUST NOT be dropped because the page as a whole reads like a form.

Cases the relation test does not settle on its own

The relation test alone MUST NOT decide these cases; each is governed by its own rule:

  • forms and ungridded key-value (Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1)
  • trailing totals outside a frame (Bottom Edge Totals and Islands§9.7.1)
  • a printed data grid under a chart (Chart With a Printed Data Grid§9.1.2)
  • detached aligned cells

Why the cost runs both ways

A missed legend makes a real relation vanish from the output (never drop). A decorative box rendered as a table asserts structure the page never claimed (never invent). Neither error is recoverable downstream, which is why the relation test — not the border, not the alignment — decides.

❌ Counter-sample — two-column author biographies

Two columns, each with bold labels — Name:, Affiliation:, Address:, Main Works: — and values beneath them, separated by horizontal rules top and bottom. Every visual cue says table: aligned label column, ruled boundaries, repeated schema across the two halves.

It is not one. The two columns are independent biographies, not two records of one relation, and the rule lines are section dividers rather than a grid. Reading it as a table would pair Marcus Ainsley with Priya Delacroix as though they shared a row.

The label/value blocks inside each column are ungridded key-value content — see Forms and Key-Value Regions§10.1 — and the bulleted publication lists are ordinary lists. The columns are unrolled in reading order, left biography first.
